title: Deploy to Kubernetes
description: Run an app on Kubernetes: a Deployment for the pods, a Service in front of them and an Ingress that brings web traffic in, with the labels and ports that tie them together.
outcomes: Pick the namespace your Kubernetes files go to
Describe a Deployment: image, replicas, port and labels
Put a Service in front of it and make its selector match
Route a host name to the Service with an Ingress
Spot a Service or Ingress that points at nothing

steps.intro: Let's put a web app on Kubernetes. We'll write three files that work as a chain: an Ingress sends traffic to a Service, and the Service sends it to the pods of a Deployment. Most broken deployments are a broken link in that chain, so we'll look closely at the links.
steps.name: A fresh project first.
steps.namespaceBadge: See this badge in the header? It's the project's default namespace. A namespace is a folder inside the cluster: names only need to be unique within one, and teams use them to keep apps and environments apart.
steps.namespaceWhy: Set it before adding anything. Every Kubernetes file kikx writes takes this namespace unless you override it on that component.
steps.namespaceTask: Your turn: click the ns badge, change the namespace to shop-prod and save.
steps.namespaceType: Type the new namespace and save.
steps.namespaceScope: Only the Deployment, Service and Ingress use it. Inventories, playbooks and Terraform ignore it. If you change it later, components already added keep the old value until you open and save them again.
steps.deployment: Now the Deployment. It tells Kubernetes which container to run and how many copies to keep alive. If a pod crashes or a node dies, Kubernetes starts a new one to get back to that number.
steps.deploymentName: The name matters more than it looks: kikx also uses it as the app label on every pod, app: shop. Remember that label, the Service will need it.
steps.image: The image is what runs in each pod. Pin a version tag rather than latest, so every pod runs the same code and a rollback means going back one tag.
steps.replicas: Replicas is how many identical pods run at once. Three lets one die or be updated while the other two keep serving.
steps.containerPort: The port is where the app listens inside the container. It's written as containerPort, and the Service will have to send traffic to exactly this number.
steps.namespaceField: This Namespace field is the per component override. Left empty, it uses the project default we just set.
steps.labels: Labels are key value tags. Extra ones like tier: web help you filter with kubectl and group things in dashboards.
steps.appLine: In the preview, app: shop appears three times: on the Deployment, in its selector and on the pod template. That's how the Deployment finds its own pods.
steps.containerPortLine: And here is containerPort 8080. Keep this number in mind.
steps.service: Pods come and go, and each new one gets a new IP address. A Service gives them one stable name and address, and spreads traffic across whichever pods are alive.
steps.serviceName: I'll call this Service frontend, a different name from the Deployment. Watch what that does.
steps.servicePort: Port is what other apps call: frontend on port 80.
steps.targetPort: Target port is where the Service forwards to. It must equal the containerPort, 8080, or connections are refused.
steps.serviceSelector: Here's the catch. The selector says app: frontend, because kikx defaults it to the Service name. But our pods are labelled app: shop. This Service selects nothing.
steps.addService: Kubernetes would accept this file without complaint. Let's add it anyway and see if kikx notices.
steps.checks: Checks reads all components together, the way the cluster would.
steps.issue: There it is: Service frontend selects app=frontend, but no deployment's pods carry those labels. Its endpoints would be empty and every request would fail. The same check warns when an Ingress routes to a Service that isn't in the project.
steps.fixTask: Your turn: fix it without renaming. Open the Service from this warning, add the label app with the value shop, and save. The warning in the Checks tab should disappear.
steps.fixOpen: Open the Service from the warning.
steps.fixLabel: Add the label app: shop. A Service selects pods by its app label, so this overrides the default selector.
steps.fixed: The selector now reads app: shop and the warning is gone. Name, labels and selector must line up, or traffic goes nowhere.
steps.ingress: Last link: the Ingress. A Service is only reachable inside the cluster. An Ingress lets the cluster's ingress controller route outside HTTP traffic to it, by host name and path.
steps.ingressTask: Left empty, the backend defaults to the Ingress name, shop, and no Service has that name. Your turn: set the host to shop.example.com and the backend service to frontend. Leave the path as /, which matches every URL on that host, and the port as 80, the Service's port.
steps.ingressHost: The host is the domain people will type. Your DNS has to point it at the cluster's ingress controller.
steps.ingressBackend: The backend is the Service by name. It must match exactly, so pick it from the suggestions.
steps.hostLine: The rule starts with the host: requests for shop.example.com land here.
steps.backendLine: And they go to the Service named frontend, on port 80. Ingress port 80, Service port 80, target port 8080, containerPort 8080: each hop must agree with the next.
steps.diagram: Architecture draws the chain we just built.
steps.diagramRead: The Ingress routes to the Service, and the Service selects the Deployment. A missing arrow here means a broken link.
steps.checksClear: And Checks has nothing left to report.
steps.done: That's a complete app on Kubernetes: a Deployment, a Service whose selector matches its pods, and an Ingress pointing at the Service, all in one namespace. Export it and apply it with kubectl apply.

recap: The project namespace applies to every Deployment, Service and Ingress unless a component sets its own.
A Deployment keeps a number of identical pods running from one image, labelled app with its name.
A Service finds pods by its selector; the labels must match or it routes nowhere.
Ports chain together: Ingress to Service port, Service target port to containerPort.
An Ingress routes a host and path to a Service by name, and Checks warns when that Service is missing.
